condition: Severe pre-eclampsia / HELLP syndrome presenting as RUQ pain
permutationLabel: 34 weeks, epigastric/RUQ pain referred as "gallbladder" (base case)
summary: 33-year-old primigravida at 34 weeks referred to the surgeons as "?biliary colic": 12 h epigastric/RUQ pain, vomiting, headache; BP 168/112, proteinuria 3+, platelets 72, ALT 312, LDH 820; gallbladder normal on US. HELLP syndrome: obstetric emergency (magnesium, antihypertensive, delivery).

inputs.chiefComplaint: Upper abdominal pain and vomiting, 34 weeks pregnant
inputs.hpi: Primigravida at 34 weeks referred as "?gallbladder". 12 hours of constant epigastric and right upper quadrant pain, vomiting three times, frontal headache since this morning and "flashing lights". Swollen face and hands for 3 days. Booking BP 118/74. Baby moving.

exam.general: BP 168/112, repeated 164/110. HR 96, RR 18, SpO2 98%. Facial and hand oedema.
exam.abdomen: Tender epigastrium and RUQ, no guarding; fundus 33 cm, uterus soft and non-tender.
exam.neuro: Brisk reflexes with 3 beats of ankle clonus.

imaging.name: USS abdomen
imaging.result: Gallbladder thin-walled, no gallstones, CBD 4 mm. Liver echotexture normal, no subcapsular haematoma.

confirmedDiagnosis.name: Severe pre-eclampsia with HELLP syndrome at 34 weeks
confirmedDiagnosis.assessmentText: Pre-eclampsia with severe features and HELLP (platelets 72, ALT 312, LDH 820) at 34 weeks — not biliary. Obstetric emergency: IV magnesium sulfate, labetalol/nifedipine for BP ≥ 160/110, CTG, delivery planning; no cholecystectomy.

socratesAnswers.associated: Nausea, vomiting, headache, flashing lights, swelling

mustNotMiss.knownGapNote: PANE has no pre-eclampsia/HELLP disease node (pane-engine has 130 diseases, none for pre-eclampsia/HELLP); top 3: acute cholecystitis (0.32), peptic ulcer, appendicitis. Symptom inference has no pre-eclampsia either (its #4 is hypertensive emergency). Nothing combines pregnancy + BP ≥ 160/110 + RUQ pain + low platelets; O14.23 maps to no protocol.
mustNotMiss.proposedFix: Add a pre-eclampsia/HELLP rule for pregnancy ≥ 20 weeks or postpartum ≤ 6 weeks with BP ≥ 140/90 (≥ 160/110 severe) plus headache, visual disturbance, epigastric/RUQ pain, proteinuria, platelets < 100 or raised transaminases → obstetric emergency (NICE NG133 / ACOG PB 222).

redFlags.note: BP 168/112 in pregnancy is severe hypertension (≥ 160/110) and needs treatment within the hour.
redFlags.knownGapNote: No hypertension flag: adaptiveTriage has no high-BP vital red flag at all, and the hypertensive_urgency prompt starts at SBP ≥ 180, so BP 164–168/110–112 in pregnancy (severe range ≥ 160/110) raises nothing.
redFlags.proposedFix: Add a BP ≥ 160/110 in-pregnancy/postpartum red flag (treat within the hour) to adaptiveTriage and computeClinicalPrompts.

mustInclude.knownGapNote: No antihypertensive suggested: BP below the 180 prompt threshold; no pregnancy-specific agents (labetalol/nifedipine) anywhere.

No obstetric output: O14.23 maps to no protocol, so the Assessment panel and Plan are empty; the prompts are biliary (MRCP, ERCP, 'HPB surgical review — Whipple') and gynaecological ('if ectopic suspected').

mustExclude.note: Normal gallbladder; RUQ pain is hepatic (HELLP). A cholecystectomy plan is a wrong-procedure suggestion.
mustExclude.knownGapNote: Web: the gallstone prompt ('Cholecystitis / gallstone disease — surgical indication') still fires from the ultrasound report although it says 'no gallstones', and adds 'Consent: laparoscopic cholecystectomy' and a full cholecystectomy operative plan; the dilated-CBD prompt fires on 'CBD 4 mm' (MRCP, ERCP, Whipple review).
mustExclude.proposedFix: Gate the cholecystectomy template on a biliary working diagnosis and on affirmed stones; parse the CBD diameter before the dilated-CBD prompt.

mustExclude.note: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are fetotoxic and not used in pregnancy.
NSAIDs are avoided at 34 weeks and with thrombocytopenia.
mustExclude.knownGapNote: Web: the cholecystectomy operative-plan template prescribes 'paracetamol 1g QDS (regular) + ibuprofen 400mg TDS (if eGFR normal)' at 34 weeks with platelets 72.
mustExclude.proposedFix: When pregnancy is recorded: strip NSAIDs from 20 weeks, replace 'β-HCG confirmed negative' with the gestation, add obstetric review and fetal monitoring to the operative templates.

guideline.name: NICE NG133 — hypertension in pregnancy: diagnosis and management
guideline.section: Pre-eclampsia with severe hypertension or features (e.g. severe headache, visual disturbance, epigastric/RUQ pain, low platelets, raised transaminases, HELLP): admit under obstetric care; antihypertensives labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa (ACE inhibitors and ARBs are not used in pregnancy); IV magnesium sulfate in severe pre-eclampsia when birth is planned or eclampsia is a concern; postnatal pre-eclampsia is managed with enalapril, nifedipine/amlodipine or labetalol
guideline.citation: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence. Hypertension in pregnancy: diagnosis and management. NICE guideline NG133, 2019 (updated 2023).

guideline.name: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 222 — gestational hypertension and preeclampsia
guideline.section: Severe features: SBP ≥ 160 or DBP ≥ 110, platelets < 100 × 10⁹/L, transaminases twice normal or severe persistent RUQ/epigastric pain, new cerebral or visual disturbance; HELLP syndrome; magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis; acute-onset severe hypertension treated urgently (labetalol, hydralazine, nifedipine); delivery at ≥ 34 weeks with severe features or HELLP; postpartum preeclampsia may present up to 6 weeks after birth
guideline.citation: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists. Gestational hypertension and preeclampsia: ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 222. Obstet Gynecol. 2020;135:e237–e260.

guideline.name: FDA drug safety communication — NSAIDs at 20 weeks or later in pregnancy
guideline.section: Avoid NSAIDs from 20 weeks of pregnancy (fetal renal dysfunction, oligohydramnios; ductal constriction later in pregnancy)
guideline.citation: US Food and Drug Administration. FDA recommends avoiding use of NSAIDs in pregnancy at 20 weeks or later because they can result in low amniotic fluid. Drug Safety Communication, 15 October 2020.

rationale: HELLP syndrome and severe pre-eclampsia commonly present as epigastric/RUQ pain and are referred as biliary disease. The priority is recognition, seizure prophylaxis, urgent BP control with pregnancy-safe agents and obstetric delivery planning — not a cholecystectomy.
